questions.q: What is the difference between an executive order and a law?
questions.searched: executive order vs law passed by congress
questions.brief: A law is passed by Congress and signed by the President (or passed over a veto); an executive order is a written directive from the President, mainly to officials in the executive branch, that rests on authority the Constitution or a law gives the President and cannot override a law. The office ("the President", "a later President"), not named presidents; give no examples that name one.

sources.label: Congressional Research Service, Executive Orders: An Introduction

questions.q: What is the difference between an executive order and a presidential memorandum?
questions.brief: Both are written presidential directives and the difference is mostly one of form: executive orders are numbered and must be published in the Federal Register, memoranda need not be; neither has more legal force by its name alone. The office ("the President", "a later President"), not named presidents; give no examples that name one.

sources.label: Congressional Research Service, Executive Orders: An Introduction

questions.q: What is the difference between an executive order and a proclamation?
questions.brief: Orders tend to be directed at government officials and proclamations at private parties (and include ceremonial ones), but there is no strict legal difference in their force. The office ("the President", "a later President"), not named presidents; give no examples that name one.

sources.label: Congressional Research Service, Executive Orders: An Introduction

questions.brief: How a draft order is prepared and reviewed under the standing rules: proposed by an agency or the White House, submitted to the Office of Management and Budget, which circulates it for comment, and reviewed by the Attorney General's Office of Legal Counsel for form and legality before the President signs it. questions.q: Who can overturn an executive order?
questions.searched: who can overturn an executive order
questions.brief: A later President (or the same one) can revoke or change it; Congress can override it by passing a law, subject to a veto; courts can strike it down if it exceeds the President's authority. The office ("the President", "a later President"), not named presidents; give no examples that name one.

sources.label: Congressional Research Service, Executive Orders: An Introduction
